The Castin leatherjacket Oligoplites saliens is a coastal carangid whose early life history is characterized by rapid development at warm temperatures. Yolk-sac larvae emerge from pelagic eggs after an incubation period of approximately 3.2 days [ab = approximately 3.2 days] when reared at 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], a duration that aligns with estimates for other tropical carangids and reflects the accelerated developmental rate typical of small-bodied pelagic teleosts inhabiting warm nearshore waters. Newly hatched larvae carry an initial dry mass of roughly 0.000268 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.000268 grams], a value derived from an egg diameter near 0.8 millimeters, reflecting the modest maternal investment typical of small-bodied pelagic spawners. This minimal provisioning at the onset of development imposes strong selective pressure on growth efficiency during the subsequent larval phase. The transition to exogenous feeding occurs within about 24 hours of eclosion, a critical window during which the yolk reserves are fully consumed and the larva must locate suitable planktonic prey to sustain growth and survival through the subsequent flexional and postflexional stages. Mortality rates during this interval are typically high, as is common among marine teleosts with small, pelagic eggs.

Somatic growth proceeds steadily during the pelagic larval phase, and by the time of metamorphosis and eventual juvenile recruitment, body size increases considerably. Upon reaching the post-settlement juvenile stage, individuals initiate a prolonged period of rapid mass gain that culminates in the attainment of the species' maximum recorded fork length, which stands at 50 centimeters [Li = 50 centimeters]. This ultimate length serves as a key benchmark for comparative life-history analyses within the Carangidae, as it correlates closely with asymptotic body mass. Growth rates appear to be strongly influenced by water temperature and prey availability, though the available data suggest that under typical coastal conditions, the trajectory toward the maximum size is completed within the first several years of life. The relatively modest maximum length, compared to larger predatory carangids such as those in the genus Caranx that can exceed one meter, places O. saliens among the smaller-bodied members of its family, a characteristic associated with its opportunistic foraging ecology and shorter generation times.

The onset of reproductive activity is tightly linked to somatic size rather than strictly to chronological age. Males and females first reach functional sexual maturity upon attaining a fork length of approximately 25 centimeters [Lp = approximately 25 centimeters], which corresponds to a wet body mass of about 95.4 grams [Wwp = about 95.4 grams] based on the length-mass conversion equation applied to this species. The congruence between length at puberty and the associated weight at puberty underscores the isometric relationship governing maturation in many carangids. Individuals below this size threshold remain reproductively inactive, directing ingested energy exclusively toward somatic growth and lipid storage. The consistency of this size–maturity relationship across populations suggests a robust physiological constraint shaped by predation risk and foraging opportunities in coastal ecosystems. This size-based threshold contrasts with age-dependent maturation schedules observed in more piscivorous carangids, where delayed maturity is compensated by larger body size and higher fecundity per spawning event.

When size at maturation is surpassed, the gonads begin seasonal cycles of recrudescence and regression. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) for reproductively active adults averages approximately 3% [GSI = approximately 3%] at a water temperature of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C]. This pattern is consistent with a multiple-batch spawning strategy, in which females produce several clutches over an extended breeding season rather than investing heavily in a single massive pulse of eggs. The index was inferred from comparative observations on the closely related Scomberoides commersonnianus, highlighting the utility of congeneric data when direct measurements on O. saliens remain limited. Seasonal variation in GSI likely tracks cycles of upwelling and plankton productivity that govern larval feeding success and, consequently, optimal timing for egg release in coastal environments.

Longevity records for Oligoplites saliens indicate that the maximum lifespan observed in coastal populations is approximately 11 years [am = approximately 11 years] under ambient thermal conditions of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], a duration that places the species among the shorter-lived members of the carangid lineage, which includes piscivorous jacks capable of surviving two decades or more. The maximum attainable wet body mass, recorded for individuals that reach the ultimate fork length, is about 733 grams [Wwi = about 733 grams], a value derived from the same allometric equation linking length to weight. This combination of moderate body size, relatively brief lifespan, and iteroparous reproduction defines the life-history strategy of O. saliens as one predicated on high annual reproductive output and rapid population turnover, well suited to its dynamic nearshore environment. The congruence between the observed maximum mass and the allometric prediction supports the utility of length-weight regressions for estimating body size in data-limited fisheries assessments of this species.
